claim: BYSMV infection induced formation of cytoplasm inclusions containing condensed ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).
source: In agreement with animal NSR viruses (Hoenen et al., 2012; Rincheval et al., 2017), BYSMV infection induced formation of cytoplasm inclusions containing condensed ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior work on animal NSR viruses.

claim: Gold particles specifically labeled the cytoplasm viroplasm in BYSMV-infected stems.
source: We further performed immunoelectron microscopy using BYSMV P antibodies and demonstrated that gold particles specifically labeled the cytoplasm viroplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only GFP-P, rather than ECFP-N or L-mCherry, formed spherical granules throughout the cytoplasm.
source: At 2 days post infiltration (dpi), confocal imaging revealed that only GFP-P, rather than ECFP-N or L-mCherry, formed spherical granules throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 1B; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1B and video.

claim: ECFP-N and L-mCherry proteins were recruited into GFP-P spherical granules.
source: Furthermore, ECFP-N and L-mCherry proteins were recruited into GFP-P spherical granules, whereas CFP-N and L-mCherry failed to form condensates with free GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: BYSMV P is the scaffold factor for formation of spherical granules and recruits the N and L proteins into condensed RNPs.
source: These results suggest that BYSMV P is the scaffold factor for formation of spherical granules and then recruits the N and L proteins into condensed RNPs to facilitate viral infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only P forms granules and recruits N and L proteins.

claim: Approximately 56.7% of GFP-P granule signal gradually recovered within 150 s after photobleaching.
source: After photobleaching, approximately 56.7% of GFP-P granule signal gradually recovered within 150 s (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—video 2), indicating a rapid redistribution of the GFP-P protein between the membraneless granules and the surrounding cellular proteins.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: GFP-P granules moved in the cytoplasm to fuse with each other.
source: In addition, these GFP-P granules moved in the cytoplasm to fuse with each other (Figure 1E; Figure 1—video 1), and treatment with 1,6-hexanediol (HEX), a chemical inhibitor of liquid-like droplets, efficiently dispersed the GFP-P granules (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1E and video.

claim: Treatment with 1,6-hexanediol efficiently dispersed the GFP-P granules.
source: In addition, these GFP-P granules moved in the cytoplasm to fuse with each other (Figure 1E; Figure 1—video 1), and treatment with 1,6-hexanediol (HEX), a chemical inhibitor of liquid-like droplets, efficiently dispersed the GFP-P granules (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data after HEX treatment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The BYSMV P protein forms liquid-like granules through LLPS in vivo.
source: Thus, these results demonstrate that the BYSMV P protein forms liquid-like granules through LLPS in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from FRAP, fusion, and HEX treatment experiments.

claim: GFP-P granules are tethered tightly to the ER network and their dynamics were correlated over time.
source: Time-lapse confocal imaging analyses showed that GFP-P granules are tethered tightly to the ER network and that their dynamics were correlated over time (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Treatment with latrunculin B reduced both ER streaming and trafficking of BYSMV-P granules.
source: Treatment with the actin-depolymerizing agent latrunculin B (LatB) reduced both ER streaming and trafficking of BYSMV-P granules (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by imaging data after LatB treatment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GFP-P granules moved along actin filaments marked by GFP-ABD2-GFP.
source: Time-lapse confocal analyses also consistently showed that GFP-P granules moved along actin filaments marked by GFP-ABD2-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The BYSMV-P granules move rapidly and fuse with each other during ER streaming in an actin-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that the BYSMV-P granules move rapidly and fuse with each other during ER streaming in an actin-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from LatB treatment and actin filament tracking experiments.

claim: Co-expression of spGFP1-10-P and 4× spGFP11-UBC32 formed GFP-labeled bodies that overlapped with the ER marker, CNX-RFP.
source: Only co-expression of spGFP1-10-P and 4× spGFP11-UBC32 formed GFP-labeled bodies that overlapped with the ER marker, CNX-RFP (Figure 1H and I; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by split-GFP complementation data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: The GFP-P granules were formed through tethering to the tubular ER network at molecular distances.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the GFP-P granules were formed through tethering to the tubular ER network at molecular distances.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from split-GFP complementation experiments showing ER contact sites.

claim: GFP-P, rather than GFP, underwent phase separation and formed granules in protoplasts of maize and barley.
source: In consistence, GFP-P, rather than GFP, underwent phase separation and formed granules in protoplasts of maize and barley, as well as protoplasts isolated from rBYSMV-RFP-infected barley leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in protoplasts shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The GFP-P protein of Northern cereal mosaic virus had similar liquid spherical granule features.
source: In addition, the GFP-P protein of a closely related Cytorhabdovirus, Northern cereal mosaic virus, had similar of liquid spherical granule features (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by imaging and FRAP data for NCMV P shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The GFP-P protein was able to condense into spherical droplets in vitro.
source: As expected, the GFP-P protein, but not GFP, was able to condense into spherical droplets (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phase separation assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Treatment with 5% HEX efficiently dispersed the GFP-P droplets in vitro.
source: Moreover, treatment with HEX (5%) efficiently dispersed the GFP-P droplets (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro HEX treatment data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased GFP-P concentration and decreased NaCl concentration enhanced numbers and sizes of GFP-P droplets.
source: Moreover, increased GFP-P concentration and decreased NaCl concentration enhanced numbers and sizes of GFP-P droplets (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phase separation assays at different concentrations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Approximately 45% of the GFP-P signal in the droplets gradually recovered within 400 s after photobleaching in vitro.
source: We further exploited FRAP to quantify molecular dynamics within the GFP-P droplets by showing that ~45% of the GFP-P signal in the droplets gradually recovered within 400 s after photobleaching (Figure 2D and E; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Supported by in vitro FRAP data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Two approaching GFP-P droplets fused into a bigger droplet in vitro.
source: In addition, we observed that two approaching GFP-P droplets fused into a bigger droplet (Figure 2F; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by in vitro time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The BYSMV P protein alone can undergo phase separation in vitro.
source: In summary, these in vitro results confirm that the BYSMV P protein alone can undergo phase separation in vitro.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro droplet formation, FRAP, and fusion experiments.

claim: When mCherry-N was incubated with GFP-P, the mCherry-N protein was gradually incorporated into GFP-P-formed droplets.
source: However, when mCherry-N was incubated with GFP-P, the mCherry-N protein was gradually incorporated into GFP-P-formed droplets (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-incubation imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both mCherry-N and Cy5-Trailer were incorporated into the GFP-P droplets in vitro.
source: As expected, both mCherry-N and Cy5-Trailer were incorporated into the GFP-P droplets, whereas they appeared to be evenly distributed when incubated with GFP (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-incubation imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BYSMV P-formed liquid droplets can incorporate BYSMV N and the 5′ trailer of BYSMV genome in vitro.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that BYSMV P-formed liquid droplets can incorporate BYSMV N and the 5′ trailer of BYSMV genome in vitro.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro incorporation experiments with N protein and RNA.

claim: The BYSMV P protein contains three IDRs according to PONDR predictions.
source: In silico predictions via PONDR suggest that the BYSMV P protein contains three IDRs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Five highly phosphorylated Ser residues are present in an SR motif located in the middle IDR of BYSMV P.
source: Interestingly, five highly phosphorylated Ser residues (amino acids 189, 191, 194, 195, and 198) are present in an SR motif (189SASRPSSIAS198) located in the middle IDR of BYSMV P (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by prior phosphorylation mapping study cited.

claim: GFP-PS5A formed relative fewer but larger granules compared to GFP-PWT.
source: Intriguingly, in contrast to GFP-PWT (~111 granules per view, >0.2 μm2), GFP-PS5A formed relative fewer (~67 granules per view) but larger granules, whereas GFP-PS5D formed very fewer granules (~17 granules per view) and more evenly located in the cytoplasm (Figure 4B and C, and large views in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Approximately 33.3% GFP-PS5A granules had larger areas (>2 μm2) compared to 16.4% of GFP-PWT granules.
source: Statistical analyses revealed that the sizes of about 16.4% of the GFP-PWT granules were larger than 2 μm2 in diameter, whereas approximately 33.3% GFP-PS5A granules had larger areas (>2 μm2) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of granule sizes shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Approximately 60% of the GFP-PS5A granule signals gradually recovered within 150 s after photobleaching.
source: In consistence with GFP-PWT (Figure 1C and D), the FRAP assays showed that approximately 60% of the GFP-PS5A granule signals gradually recovered within 150 s after photobleaching (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data for PS5A mutant shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two bands of GFP-PWT corresponding to about 72 kD (P72) and 74 kD (P74) were present in the samples.
source: Interestingly, two bands of GFP-PWT corresponding to about 72 kD (P72) and 74 kD (P74) were present in the samples, whereas GFP-PS5A and GFP-PS5D existed as P72 and P74, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The GFP-PS5D protein was mainly concentrated in the supernatant fraction, while the GFP-PS5A protein was mainly in the pellet fraction.
source: As expected, the GFP-PS5D protein was mainly concentrated in the supernatant fraction, while the GFP-PS5A protein was mainly in the pellet fraction (Figure 4F), indicating that GFP-PS5D and GFP-PS5A primarily existed as soluble and condensed states, respectively.
evidence: Supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GFP-PWT and GFP-PS5A, but not GFP-PS5D, underwent phase separation in 150 mM NaCl in vitro.
source: The results were consistent with the in vivo results (Figure 4B), as GFP-PWT and GFP-PS5A, but not GFP-PS5D, underwent phase separation in 150 mM NaCl (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phase separation assays shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The solution turbidity values of the condensed droplets from GFP-PS5A and GFP-PWT were higher than that of free GFP.
source: As expected, the solution turbidity values of the condensed droplets from GFP-PS5A and GFP-PWT were higher than that of free GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by turbidity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Phosphorylation of the SR region within the middle IDR of BYSMV P significantly impairs phase separation in vivo and in vitro.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that phosphorylation of the SR region within the middle IDR of BYSMV P significantly impairs phase separation in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparing WT, PS5A, and PS5D mutants in vivo and in vitro.

claim: Most of the GFP-PWT granules were dispersed upon co-expression of NbCK1.3.
source: As expected, most of the GFP-PWT granules were dispersed upon co-expression of NbCK1.3, while GFP-PS5A granules were not obviously affected by NbCK1.3 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data with CK1 co-expression shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-expression of NbCK1.3 drastically decreased the hypophosphorylated P72 form of GFP-PWT.
source: Western blotting analyses showed that co-expression of NbCK1.3 drastically decreased the hypophosphorylated P72 form of GFP-PWT compared with equal accumulation of P72 and P74 forms during co-expression of GFP-PWT and EV (Figure 5B, compare lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The P72 form of GFP-PS5A and the P74 form of GFP-PS5D were not affected by co-expression of either NbCK1.3 or EV.
source: In contrast, the P72 form of GFP-PS5A and the P74 form of GFP-PS5D were not affected by co-expression of either NbCK1.3 or EV (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Host NbCK1 inhibits BYSMV P phase separation mainly by phosphorylating the five Ser residues of the SR motif within the middle IDR region of BYSMV P.
source: These results indicate that host NbCK1 inhibits BYSMV P phase separation mainly by phosphorylating the five Ser residues of the SR motif within the middle IDR region of BYSMV P (Figure 4A).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CK1 co-expression experiments with WT and mutant P proteins.

claim: Overexpression of NbCK1.3DN did not affect phosphorylation and phase separation of GFP-PWT compared with NbCK1.3.
source: As expected, overexpression of NbCK1.3DN did not affect phosphorylation and phase separation of GFP-PWT compared with NbCK1.3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging and Western blotting data with kinase-dead mutant shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The purified GFP-PWT protein underwent phase separation when co-expressed with NbCK1.3DN, but co-expression of NbCK1.3 inhibited phase separation of GFP-PWT.
source: Interestingly, the purified GFP-PWT protein underwent phase separation when co-expressed with NbCK1.3DN, but co-expression of NbCK1.3 inhibited phase separation of GFP-PWT (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phase separation assays with bacterial co-expression shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Co-expression of NbCK1.3, rather than NbCK1.3DN, resulted in production of the upper P74 band of GFP-PWT.
source: In addition, the SDS-PAGE gel showed that co-expression of NbCK1.3, rather than NbCK1.3DN, resulted in production of the upper P74 band of GFP-PWT (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: P74 represents hyper-phosphorylated forms of GFP-PWT elicited by co-expressed NbCK1.3.
source: Moreover, we failed to detect the P74 band of GFP-PWT after λ-protein phosphatase (λPPase) treatment in vitro (Figure 5E), indicating that P74 represents hyper-phosphorylated forms of GFP-PWT elicited by co-expressed NbCK1.3.
evidence: Supported by phosphatase treatment data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Host CK1 proteins inhibit phase separation of BYSMV P by phosphorylating the SR region of the BYSMV P middle IDR.
source: Collectively, host CK1 proteins inhibit phase separation of BYSMV P by phosphorylating the SR region of the BYSMV P middle IDR.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CK1 co-expression, kinase-dead mutant, and phosphatase treatment experiments.

claim: The numbers of RFP foci in the GFP-PS5A samples were significantly higher than those of GFP-PWT, whereas GFP-PS5D expression resulted in a reduced number of RFP foci.
source: Furthermore, the numbers of RFP foci in the GFP-PS5A samples were significantly higher than those of GFP-PWT, whereas GFP-PS5D expression resulted in a reduced number of RFP foci (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by minireplicon assay imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RFP accumulation was highest after GFP-PS5A expression, followed by GFP-PWT and GFP-PS5D.
source: Western blotting analyses consistently showed that RFP accumulation was highest after GFP-PS5A expression, followed by GFP-PWT and GFP-PS5D (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Accumulation of the full-length gMR was upregulated in GFP-PS5A samples but decreased in GFP-PS5D samples compared with those of GFP-PWT samples.
source: Accumulation of the full-length gMR was upregulated in GFP-PS5A samples but decreased in GFP-PS5D samples compared with those of GFP-PWT samples (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data for replication shown in Figure 6C.

claim: GFP-PS5D supported higher transcription activity but GFP-PS5A expression compromised transcription.
source: However, GFP-PS5D supported higher transcription activity but GFP-PS5A expression compromised transcription (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data for transcription shown in Figure 6D.

claim: GFP-PS5A with increased LLPS activity supports enhanced virus replication but decreased transcription.
source: Collectively, GFP-PS5A with increased LLPS activity supports enhanced virus replication but decreased transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from minireplicon assays comparing replication and transcription levels.

claim: GFP-PS5D with impaired LLPS activity inhibited virus replication but facilitated transcription.
source: In contrast, GFP-PS5D with impaired LLPS activity inhibited virus replication but facilitated transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from minireplicon assays comparing replication and transcription levels.

claim: The unphosphorylated BYSMV-P protein undergoes LLPS and forms spherical granules as viral factories to promote virus replication.
source: In summary, the unphosphorylated BYSMV-P protein undergoes LLPS and forms spherical granules as viral factories to promote virus replication.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experiments with PS5A mutant.

claim: The conserved CK1 protein kinases phosphorylate the SR region of BYSMV P to hyper-phosphorylated P forms and compromise LLPS, which results in soluble RNPs for virus transcription.
source: In contrast, the conserved CK1 protein kinases phosphorylate the SR region of BYSMV P to hyper-phosphorylated P forms and compromise LLPS, which results in soluble RNPs for virus transcription (Figure 7).
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all CK1 and PS5D experiments.

claim: The CK1-mediated phosphorylation inhibits phase separation of BYSMV P and viral replication.
source: Therefore, the CK1-mediated phosphorylation inhibits phase separation of BYSMV P and viral replication.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experiments.

claim: LLPS plays important roles in forming cellular membraneless organelles.
source: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) plays important roles in forming cellular membraneless organelles.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about LLPS.

claim: Many negative-sense RNA (NSR) viruses are known to form membraneless replication compartments, called viroplasms, viral inclusion bodies (IBs), or viral factories.
source: Many negative-sense RNA (NSR) viruses are known to form membraneless replication compartments, called viroplasms, viral inclusion bodies (IBs), or viral factories (Lahaye et al., 2009; Hoenen et al., 2012; Rincheval et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on NSR viruses.

claim: Studies about animal NSR viruses have revealed that LLPS plays important roles in viroplasm formation through concentrating viral and host components.
source: Studies about animal NSR viruses have revealed that LLPS plays important roles in viroplasm formation through concentrating viral and host components.
evidence: Summary of prior research on animal NSR viruses.

claim: The viroplasms of the rabies virus known as Negri bodies (NBs) were first reported to have the features of liquid organelles.
source: The viroplasms of the rabies virus known as Negri bodies (NBs) were first reported to have the features of liquid organelles (Nikolic et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on rabies virus.

claim: Vesicular stomatitis virus and measles virus exploit LLPS to form virus IBs.
source: Subsequent studies have shown that another two animal NSR viruses, vesicular stomatitis virus and measles virus, also exploit LLPS to form virus IBs (Heinrich et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on VSV and measles virus.

claim: The P protein of borna disease virus and the N protein of ebola virus are sufficient to elicit formation of liquid organelles alone.
source: The P protein of borna disease virus and the N protein of ebola virus are also sufficient to elicit formation of liquid organelles alone (Charlier et al., 2013; Miyake et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on borna disease virus and ebola virus.

claim: Host factors regulating LLPS of plant NSR viroplasms are still largely unknown.
source: Nonetheless, host factors regulating LLPS of plant NSR viroplasms are still largely unknown.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: BYSMV is a member of the Cytorhabdovirus genus, family Rhabdoviridae in the order Mononegavirales.
source: Barley yellow striate mosaic virus (BYSMV) is a member of the Cytorhabdovirus genus, family Rhabdoviridae in the order Mononegavirales.
evidence: Taxonomic classification of BYSMV.

claim: BYSMV infects cereal plants and severely affects crop production worldwide through persistent transmission by the small brown planthopper.
source: BYSMV infects cereal plants and severely affects crop production worldwide through persistent transmission by the small brown planthopper (Laodelphax striatellus).
evidence: Background information about BYSMV biology.

claim: The BYSMV genome encodes five structural proteins and five accessory proteins.
source: The BYSMV genome encodes five structural proteins, including the nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), and polymerase (L), as well as another five accessory proteins, in the order 3′–N–P–P3–P4/P5–P6–M–G–P9–L–5′ (Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on BYSMV genome organization.

claim: Host CK1-mediated phosphorylation of a highly serine-rich (SR) motif at the C-terminal IDR of the P protein regulates virus infection.
source: Interestingly, CK1-mediated phosphorylation of a highly serine-rich (SR) motif at the C-terminal IDR of the P protein regulates virus infection (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on CK1 phosphorylation of BYSMV P.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that a plant NSR virus uses LLPS to form viral replication center.
source: Here, we provide the first evidence, to the best of our knowledge, that a plant NSR virus uses LLPS to form viral replication center.
evidence: Authors' claim about the novelty of their findings.

claim: The NBs of rabies virus were formed through phase separation, which requires co-expression of both the N and P proteins and residues 132–150 of an intrinsically disordered domain within the P protein.
source: The NBs of rabies virus were formed through phase separation, which however requires co-expression of both the N and P proteins and residues 132–150 of an intrinsically disordered domain within the P protein (Nikolic et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on rabies virus NBs.

claim: CK2-mediated phosphorylation of zona occludens inhibits homologous phase separation in mammalian cells.
source: These results are in agreement with recent reports in mammalian cells in which CK2-mediated phosphorylation of zona occludens, a cytoplasmic scaffolding protein, inhibits homologous phase separation (Beutel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on CK2 and phase separation.

claim: The partitioning defective 3/6 (Par3/Par6) condensates are dispersed by PKC-mediated phosphorylation.
source: The partitioning defective 3/6 (Par3/Par6) condensates are also dispersed by PKC-mediated phosphorylation (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on Par3/Par6 and phosphorylation.

claim: Rhabdovirus transcription and replication complexes contain common virus replication derivatives, in which the N-RNA complex serves as a template for viral RdRp complexes comprising the P and L proteins.
source: Rhabdovirus transcription and replication complexes contain common virus replication derivatives, in which the N-RNA complex serves as a template for viral RdRp complexes comprising the P and L proteins (Ivanov et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on rhabdovirus replication.

claim: During rhabdovirus replication, the newly synthesized genome or antigenome need to be encapsidated by the N protein, which requires a continuous supply of RNA-free N molecules.
source: During rhabdovirus replication, the newly synthesized genome or antigenome need to be encapsidated by the N protein, which requires a continuous supply of RNA-free N molecules (Ivanov et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on rhabdovirus replication.

claim: LLPS of BYSMV P facilitates concentration of the BYSMV N protein into virus replication sites.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising to find that LLPS of BYSMV P facilitates concentration of the BYSMV N protein into virus replication sites.
evidence: Inference drawn from the requirement for N protein concentration during replication.

claim: Viral mRNAs are released without N encapsidation, which results in dispersed protein rather than condensed N protein in virus transcription sites.
source: In contrast, viral mRNAs are released without N encapsidation, which results in dispersed protein rather than condensed N protein in virus transcription sites (Figure 7).
evidence: Inference drawn from the difference between replication and transcription processes.

claim: The phosphorylation of the BYSMV P SR region by host CK1s abrogates the liquid-like membraneless viroplasms and subsequently drives the switch from virus replication to transcription.
source: Therefore, we propose that the phosphorylation of the BYSMV P SR region by host CK1s abrogates the liquid-like membraneless viroplasms and subsequently drives the switch from virus replication to transcription.
evidence: Proposed model based on all experimental findings.

claim: ER contact sites regulate the biogenesis and fission of processing bodies (PBs) and liquid spherical stress granules.
source: For instance, ER contact sites regulate the biogenesis and fission of two important membraneless organelles, processing bodies (PBs) and liquid spherical stress granules (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on ER contact sites.

claim: mRNA translation inhibition facilitates formation of PB condensates, whereas increasing the translational activity induces PB disassembly.
source: More interestingly, mRNA translation inhibition facilitates formation of PB condensates, whereas increasing the translational activity induces PB disassembly, indicating that the ER contact sites may shuttle mRNAs between the ER and PBs (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on PB dynamics.

claim: The ER/actin network acts as a platform to facilitate trafficking and fusion of the GFP-P granules.
source: In the current study, we observed that the ER/actin network acts as a platform to facilitate trafficking and fusion of the GFP-P granules (Figure 1G; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: ER-viroplasm contact sites are conduits for viral protein and mRNA exchange between the two organelles.
source: Given that viroplasms need large amount of BYSMV N to encapsidate newly synthesized genomic/antigenomic RNAs, the BYSMV P-mediated condensates on the ER/actin network opens up the possibility that ER-viroplasm contact sites are conduits for viral protein and mRNA exchange between the two organelles.
evidence: Speculative inference about the function of ER-viroplasm contact sites.

claim: The BYSMV P condensates tether on the ER tubules and are dispersed by CK1-mediated phosphorylation, subsequently stimulating virus transcription and transporting viral mRNAs to the ER for efficient translation.
source: Taken together, we propose that the BYSMV P condensates tether on the ER tubules and are dispersed by CK1-mediated phosphorylation. Subsequently, virus transcription is stimulated and viral mRNAs are transported to the ER for efficient translation.
evidence: Proposed model integrating all findings.
